analysis.one_liner: Restricts aggressive medical debt collection and creates a public database of debt collectors.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote or floor action, dying in the Senate health committee despite being introduced by a Democrat with a Republican cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would place new limits on how hospitals, clinics, and their debt collectors pursue unpaid medical bills. Providers would have to pause extraordinary collection actions—like lawsuits, wage garnishment, or credit reporting—while a patient's insurance appeal is pending, check whether the patient qualifies for charity care or public assistance before collecting, and wait 180 days after the first bill before taking extraordinary action. Patients would get plain-language itemized bills, payment receipts, and language help, and a public database would disclose which debt collectors hospitals use and whom they pursue, broken down by race, gender, and ZIP code.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients carrying medical debt gain the most. They would get breathing room before aggressive collection starts (180 days after the first bill), collections would have to stop during insurance appeals, hospitals would have to screen for charity care or public program eligibility before collecting, and uninsured patients treated by nonprofit hospitals could not be charged more than the "generally billed" amount. Itemized statements, payment receipts, and language-assistance notices would make bills easier to understand and dispute. Civil penalties (actual damages, up to $1,000 per violation for individuals, class caps of $2 million or 1% of net income, plus attorney's fees) give patients a way to enforce these rights. The public database would also give regulators and journalists visibility into who is being pursued for medical debt and how [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: Collections would be halted whenever a patient notifies the provider that an insurance appeal is pending, so patients would not be pursued for bills while coverage decisions are still being contested.

Before any collection activity, providers would have to determine whether the patient qualifies for a federal or state program or the provider's own charity care, and refer the patient to that assistance—moving many bills off the books before they become collections cases.

Extraordinary collection actions (wage garnishment, bank account attachments, liens, credit reporting, lawsuits) would be barred until 180 days after the first bill is sent, giving patients time to resolve or dispute charges.

Patients would receive easy-to-understand itemized statements before collection begins, detailed receipts within 30 days of any payment, and information about free language assistance, making bills easier to check and challenge.
Nonprofit hospitals could no longer bill uninsured patients more than the amount generally billed to insured patients, closing the gap where the uninsured face the highest prices.

A public, searchable database would disclose which debt collectors each health entity uses or sells debt to, the types and number of collection actions taken, and breakdowns by race, ethnicity, gender, and ZIP code—exposing who bears the brunt of medical debt collection—and the CFPB would report regularly on the medical debt industry.

Providers or collectors who violate the rules would owe patients actual damages, up to $1,000 per violation individually, class damages capped at the lesser of $2 million or 1% of net income, plus attorney's fees.

analysis.who_pays: Hospitals (nonprofit and for-profit), clinics, physician group practices and staffing firms, nursing homes, and the medical debt collection industry would bear the cost: they would delay collections by at least 180 days, absorb bills waived after charity-care screening, cap charges to uninsured patients, produce itemized statements and receipts, and file detailed annual reports to the federal database. Some of those costs could be passed on through higher charges, and collection agencies would see fewer accounts and slower recoveries [S3].

drawbacks.text: The 180-day waiting period, mandatory charity-care screening, and detailed reporting would reduce recoveries and add administrative work for providers, and some hospitals could pass those costs on through higher charges—a cost an honest supporter should acknowledge.
The enforcement cap—class damages limited to the lesser of $2 million or 1% of the provider's annual net income—may be a small deterrent for large hospital systems with billions in revenue.

Key terms are left to the discretion of the Health and Human Services Secretary: the definition of 'health care entity' (including how small physician practices are exempted) would be developed by the Secretary, so the law's real coverage would depend on how a future administration wrote the rules.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits to patients are concrete and targeted at documented practices—suing patients, garnishing wages, and reporting medical debt while appeals are pending, and charging uninsured patients more than insured ones. The costs fall on providers and collectors in the form of delayed payments, waived charity-care bills, and paperwork, and could modestly raise charges for others. On balance the consumer protections and public transparency outweigh the compliance burden, though the bill is limited: it does not reduce medical debt itself, only how it is pursued, and its strength would depend heavily on regulations written after passage.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which never acted on it, so it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Chris Murphy introduced the bill in July 2023, joined by Senator Mike Braun, a Republican, as an original cosponsor.
It was read twice and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee—the standard first step for a health bill—and that is where the record ends.
The committee never held a markup or vote, the Senate never debated it, and it never became law before the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hospitals, physician staffing firms, and the medical debt collection industry are better off because the bill died—they avoided the 180-day collection delay, charity-care screening requirements, billing caps on uninsured patients, and public reporting. Patients with medical debt gained nothing from the outcome.

against.name: Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to a committee vote or markup; it sat without action until the Congress ended

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; the only sign of partisan shape is the sponsorship, which was bipartisan—a Democrat leading with a Republican original cosponsor.

industries.note: Hospitals would face the bill's core restrictions: a 180-day wait before extraordinary collection actions, mandatory charity-care and public-program screening before collecting, a cap on what nonprofit hospitals can charge uninsured patients, and detailed public reporting. Their interest in aggressive collection runs directly against patients' interest in breathing room and assistance screening.

Collectors would see fewer accounts referred, longer delays before action, mandatory identity verification, and public disclosure of which hospitals use them and how many lawsuits, garnishments, and liens they pursue, broken down by race and ZIP code. Their revenue depends on pursuing exactly the debts the bill would slow or erase.

industries.industry: Physician staffing firms and physician services companies
industries.note: The bill explicitly names physician staffing firms and services companies—major sources of surprise out-of-network bills—as covered health care entities subject to all the collection restrictions and reporting duties.

industries.industry: Credit reporting bureaus and consumer data industry
industries.note: The bill would restrict reporting medical debt to consumer reporting agencies until 180 days after the first bill and require the CFPB to fold anonymized data from the three largest credit bureaus into public reports on medical debt collections, increasing scrutiny of their role.
The CFPB would get a new statutory mandate to report publicly on the medical debt industry and assess using the database for its supervision of debt collectors, expanding its oversight toolkit.
